An evidence-led investigation · Canada / 2025

When a prediction is right, what have we actually learned?

Polls report intentions. Models estimate possibilities. Elections produce observable results. None, on its own, tells us why people voted as they did—or what we should decide.

What is this? An interactive research investigation of Canada’s 2025 federal election, with Toronto’s municipal elections as a separate evidence stress test. We compare polls, retrospectively reconstructed classifications, certified outcomes and causal hypotheses—not to forecast the next election, but to ask which conclusions each kind of evidence can justify.

Begin the investigation ↓Methods & sources
343
Federal riding outcomes in the 2025 election. Strong evidence about recorded results—not, by themselves, about the causes of those results.
The question is not only whether a model was right. It is what we are justified in concluding.
Historical research and information-design study. No electoral endorsement, current election forecast or validated causal effect is presented. Canada and Toronto are distinct election systems.
Before the first chart · The research in brief

What are we trying to learn?

The same election can yield a polling number, a map of estimated winners, a certified result and several explanations. These are different claims, with different evidence standards. This experience follows the chain from one to the next—and asks where a responsible analyst should stop.

The investigation
  1. Measure. What did Canadian survey respondents actually report, and when?
  2. Reconstruct. How do assumptions change our historical riding classifications?
  3. Compare. What do the 343 official outcomes reveal about representation and error?
  4. Challenge. Which explanations lack the causal evidence needed to establish them?
  5. Decide. When should we report, qualify or withhold a conclusion?
Study boundaries

Primary case: Canada’s 2025 federal election and 343 constituencies. Linked test: Toronto municipal wards and polling archives across 2018, 2022, 2023 and 2026. These electoral systems are not pooled.

What you will discover: where apparently straightforward numbers change meaning when we inspect the denominator, geography, assumptions, historical information cutoff or strength of evidence.

Important: this is not a real-time forecast, a validated prospective forecasting model or a causal-effect study.

Act 01 · Measurement

What people tell us.

A poll records a response from a particular sample at a particular moment. It does not record a future vote.

Evidence earned · 1/5 We can report sampled intentions; we cannot yet report the electorate’s outcome.

Before Canadians voted in April 2025, survey firms reported a shifting picture of public intentions. Each release had a fieldwork period, sampling method, respondent definition and publication timeline.

Those distinctions matter. A measured share of reported intention is not an election outcome, nor a modelled probability of victory.

The measurement has meaning only when we know who was asked, when, and under what conditions.

Evidence boundary. This plot contains 63 curated survey observations from the existing research dataset, not an exhaustive or fully date-audited polling census. Explore individual records without treating the line of points as a reconstructed official polling average. AAPOR disclosure standards ↗

How this analysis works

Technique: comparative time series of 63 selected polling observations, including fieldwork dates and disclosures.

What it cannot establish: It cannot represent a complete polling universe or establish subsequent voting behaviour.

Select a point to inspect the pollster, fieldwork end date, reported respondent count and source. The release timestamp is not independently verified for all records.
Act 02 · Inference

What models predict.

Moving from polling to riding estimates requires assumptions. Every modelling choice introduces another source of uncertainty.

Evidence earned · 2/5 We now have conditional classifications; not historically validated win probabilities.

National survey shares cannot be directly converted into 343 local riding winners. Geography, historical patterns, redistribution and regional variation complicate that translation.

This research uses a retrospectively reconstructed, poll-adjusted historical rule (M1) to show how estimated classifications vary with the information cutoff. It is not a verified contemporaneous forecast, a trained probability model or a claim of prospective skill.

A category labelled “estimated winner” is not a probability of winning.

Evidence boundary. The as-of analysis assumes a three-day lag from survey fieldwork to availability; many original publication timestamps remain unaudited. The 2025 result must never be treated as an input available before election day.

Reconstructed estimate · not probability

How this analysis works

Technique: point-in-time reconstruction of M0/M1 classification rules across 343 ridings.

What it cannot establish: M1 uses assumed source timing and is not an independently archived election-night forecast or probabilistic model.

Maps are riding classifications—not predictive probabilities. Official results are revealed separately in Act III. This reconstruction is methodologically illustrative and subject to source-date limitations.
Act 03 · Observation & error

What elections reveal.

A certified result can settle what happened. It cannot, by itself, prove that a model was well calibrated or explain why the result occurred.

Evidence earned · 3/5 Observed outcomes permit error measurement; they do not identify causes.

In 2025, Canada's 343 federal ridings elected one member each. A conventional map gives large rural seats more visual area, even though each riding elects exactly one MP.

The independent 338Canada retrospective reports 299 of 343 riding winner classifications correct. That is a useful classification statistic, but it does not independently demonstrate calibrated probabilities or an identified causal mechanism.

Ask what the score measures—and what it leaves out.

Linked Toronto test. Switch the map to Toronto's 25 wards. They are different municipal geographic units. Selected ward polling evidence does not constitute a representative prediction audit. 338Canada retrospective ↗

How this analysis works

Technique: geographic choropleth, equal-seat representation, result comparison and winner-classification diagnostics.

What it cannot establish: Published third-party accuracy and the project’s illustrative model errors must not be combined into one performance metric.

Geographic area is not proportional to votes or seats. Candidate records are reconciled to published aggregates, but an independent candidate-level source audit remains pending.
Act 04 · Explanation

Why outcomes occur.

An observed association is a clue, not an explanation. Causal claims demand evidence about competing mechanisms and counterfactuals.

Evidence earned · 4/5 We can articulate hypotheses and missing tests; causation remains unidentified.

Geographic voting patterns, changing survey responses and election outcomes can support hypotheses. They cannot reveal individual motivations or isolate the effect of campaign activity without additional research designs.

The difficulty increases when a forecast itself enters public conversation. Media coverage and behaviour may interact, but demonstrating a feedback mechanism requires evidence beyond poll and vote totals.

A plausible story is not the same as an identified causal effect.

Scientific challenge. Choose an explanation to see what is observed, what remains hypothetical, and which missing evidence would help distinguish alternatives. These are research questions, not statements about why a party won.

Causal challenge · not causal inference

Three explanations. Three evidence gaps.

What would we need to know before using the word “because”?

OBSERVEDRegional vote distributionsAdministrative election records
HYPOTHESIZEDVotes concentrate geographicallyPossible mechanism, not verified cause
MISSING TESTDesign separating alternativesCounterfactual or quasi-experimental evidence
What is not established?

How this analysis works

Technique: structured competing-cause audit and counterfactual challenge.

What it cannot establish: The panel documents missing identification; no causal effects have been estimated.

The arrows are a conceptual research chain—not estimated effect sizes or proof of influence. No causal model has been fit.
Act 05 · Judgment and consequence

What are we justified in deciding?

The right question is not only “Was the model correct?” It is whether a decision was warranted, challenged, documented and improved by subsequent evidence.

Evidence earned · 5/5 We can define a defensible decision boundary; whether this improves judgment is untested.

Our proposed Decision Twin extends beyond dashboards and predictions. It would connect an evidence claim to the action it permits, the authority responsible, its uncertainty, and a receipt for later review.

At this stage, this is a design hypothesis rather than a validated intervention. The interface demonstrates an evidence discipline; it has not been experimentally shown to improve reader judgment or operational decisions.

Sometimes the most defensible decision is to qualify a claim—or decline to make it.

Future validation. Compare this guided approach against the V18.2 interface on claim classification, error interpretation, evidence retrieval, time and cognitive effort. Better visual design must be demonstrated, not declared. The Toronto historical model-fitting gate remains closed.

DECISION RECORD / EXAMPLEQUALIFY
A real decision receipt would also retain timestamped evidence, alternatives, approval, consequences and measured feedback. Those controls are proposed, not implemented here.
How this analysis works

Technique: evidence-to-action decision record with an explicit qualified/withheld conclusion.

What it cannot establish: Prescriptive benefit, decision quality and human oversight have not yet been evaluated in experiments.

The goal is a testable evidence-to-decision architecture: observation → assumption → challenge → authorized action → measured learning.
The conclusion

Evidence before certainty.
Judgment before action.

What people tell us. What models predict. What elections reveal. Why outcomes occur. What the evidence permits us to decide.

The next research question is empirical: does this design actually improve decision quality? Until that is tested, it remains a transparent proposition—not a proven solution.

Evidence Lab

Scope: Canada 2025 federal election plus separately bounded Toronto municipal research (2018, 2022, 2023, 2026). The saved V17 model-readiness protocol is not passed. This lab does not reconstruct independent prospective forecasts.

National votes versus seats

Two different denominators. The top bar represents share of valid candidate votes; the bottom bar share of 343 seats. Both are drawn against the same 0–55% scale.

Seats are not proportional-vote allocations. A larger map area is not a larger seat share.

Published performance vs reconstructed rules

The independent published retrospective and the research baselines are different objects.

Why these should not be pooled

338Canada's retrospective classification score does not supply archived individual probabilities in this package. M0 uses the 2021 transposed leading party; M1 is a retrospective poll-adjusted rule with assumed source timing. Neither demonstrates calibration.

Toronto: historical evidence permissions

Each election year answers some questions more strongly than others. Select a year to read the gate.

The original archive contains unresolved 2018/2022 records and a disputed June 2023 Liaison topline. No historical model should be fit until its prerequisites are met.

Methodological stop rule

Original poll acquisition and reconciliation → lock publication cutoffs → harmonize target and respondent universe → freeze scoring plan → evaluate only when qualified.

Current state: NOT PASSED. The historical protocol's minimum gate is three elections with two independent qualifying late pollsters per election. That is not a guarantee of statistical power.

Sources, lineage and restrictions

  1. Elections Canada, 45th General Election Official Voting Results. Research values derived from a transformed workbook, reconciled to published national aggregates; independent row-level audit is outstanding.
  2. 338Canada, 2025 retrospective. Published winner classification performance (299/343). Not a set of stored riding-level calibrated probabilities.
  3. Scotiabank Economics, April 28, 2025. Contemporaneous report of final central projected seats (187 Liberal). Not a recovered complete riding-level forecast dataset.
  4. Elections Canada geographic boundaries. Simplified polygon paths for exploration, not a geodetically precise official map product.
  5. City of Toronto election results. Municipal ward winners and mayoral official-results references are not equivalent to federal voting geography.
  6. AAPOR Transparency and Disclosure Standards. Relevant to archive quality and survey provenance.
  7. Gneiting & Raftery (2007), Strictly Proper Scoring Rules. A classification fraction alone is not probability calibration.
